section_1.title: The Problem: Average vs. Instantaneous Speed
section_1.content: Begin by reviewing 'Average Speed' (Total distance / Total time). Use a visual of a Cheetah running. Contrast this with the 'Speedometer' reading at a single, frozen moment in time. Establish the goal: How do we calculate speed at an exact instant?
section_1.example: A Cheetah sprints. We know its average speed over 10 seconds, but how fast is it going at exactly 3.5 seconds?

section_2.title: Visualizing the Limit: From Secant to Tangent
section_2.content: Introduce a position-time graph. Show a secant line connecting two points (t1, t2). As we shrink the gap between the points (Δt approaching 0), animate the secant line rotating until it becomes a tangent line. This visual transition represents the 'Limit'.
section_2.example: Two points on a curve move closer together until they merge into one, showing the slope at a single point.

section_3.title: Defining the Derivative
section_3.content: Formalize the concept. Introduce the limit definition of the derivative: f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h. Break down each component: the slope of the secant (rise/run) transforming into the slope of the tangent via the limit.
section_3.example: Representing the change in position (f(x+h) - f(x)) divided by the tiny change in time (h).

section_4.title: Application: The Falling Drone
section_4.content: Apply the derivative to a practical scenario. Use a drone dropping a package. Show how the derivative function (velocity) provides the exact speed at any height, illustrating that the derivative is the 'rate of change' function.
section_4.example: A delivery drone drops a package; the derivative of its height equation gives us the exact velocity at any point during the fall.

section_5.title: Summary and Intuition Check
section_5.content: Summarize that the 'Derivative' is simply the slope of the tangent line, which represents the 'Instantaneous Rate of Change'. Conclude with a quick visual quiz: matching derivative values (slopes) to different points on a mountain profile.
section_5.example: Looking at a mountain path: steep positive slope (climbing), zero slope (peak), negative slope (descending).
